learn.title: Renewable Purchase Obligation for DISCOMs
learn.intro: India's Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO) mandates that distribution companies purchase a minimum percentage of their power from renewable sources. This policy is critical for India's clean energy transition, ensuring demand for solar and wind projects while helping achieve the country's target of 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030.
learn.c1_text: Think of RPO like a school requiring students to read books from different genres. Just as students must include fiction, non-fiction, and poetry in their reading, Indian DISCOMs must source a portion of their electricity from renewables. Currently, the central government sets RPO targets, typically around 15-17% renewable energy in utilities' portfolios.
learn.c2_text: RPO operates under the Electricity Act 2003, enforced by state electricity regulators. Each state determines its specific RPO targets based on renewable energy potential. Non-compliance results in penalties paid to the Renewable Energy Certificate (REC) market, creating financial incentives for DISCOMs to meet their obligations.
learn.c3_text: As of 2023, India has achieved over 130 GW of renewable energy capacity, partly driven by RPO compliance. States like Gujarat and Tamil Nadu lead in meeting their obligations. However, many DISCOMs struggle financially, making RPO adherence challenging. The government introduced relaxed timelines and hybrid models to support compliance.
learn.stat1: India targets 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030
learn.stat3: RPO compliance rate varies 60-85% across states
learn.stat4: Solar alone contributes over 70 GW to renewable mix

learn.title: Solar PV Panels and Photoelectric Effect
learn.intro: Solar photovoltaic panels convert sunlight directly into electricity using the photoelectric effect—a phenomenon that revolutionized renewable energy. Understanding this process is fundamental to appreciating how solar power works, making it essential knowledge for anyone interested in clean energy technologies and their role in combating climate change.
learn.c1_text: Imagine sunlight as a stream of tiny energy packets called photons. When these photons hit a solar cell's semiconductor material (usually silicon), they knock electrons loose, allowing them to flow freely. This movement creates direct current (DC) electricity—like wind pushing sailboat blades to generate motion.
learn.c2_text: Solar cells use a p-n junction where phosphorus-doped (n-type) and boron-doped (p-type) silicon layers create an electric field. When photons with sufficient energy hit this junction, they excite electrons from the valence band to the conduction band, generating electron-hole pairs that separate due to the built-in electric field.
learn.c3_text: India's National Solar Mission launched in 2010 transformed the country into a global solar leader. From just 2.6 GW in 2010, India now has over 70 GW of solar capacity. The Bhadla Solar Park in Rajasthan spans 14,000 acres, making it one of the world's largest single-location solar installations.
learn.stat3: One solar panel can power 3-4 homes daily
learn.readLabel: Read at US Dept of Energy

learn.title: Bifacial Solar Panels Explained
learn.intro: Bifacial solar panels represent a significant advancement in solar technology, capable of generating electricity from both sides of the panel. Unlike traditional monofacial panels, they capture reflected light from the ground surface, potentially increasing energy yield by 10-30% compared to conventional panels.
learn.c1_text: Picture a book that generates electricity from both covers. Bifacial panels work similarly—they collect sunlight on the front side and reflected light (albedo) on the back. Surfaces like white concrete, sand, or snow reflect substantial light, effectively doubling the energy capture opportunity for each panel.
learn.c2_text: These panels use transparent backsheets or glass-glass construction with contacts on both sides. The rear side contains the same anti-reflective coatings and busbars as the front. Installation requires mounting systems that allow light reflection underneath, typically elevated structures or tracking systems that optimize ground reflectance capture.
learn.c3_text: India's first large-scale bifacial solar project was commissioned in Gujarat. The International Airport in Delhi uses bifacial panels for both energy generation and architectural integration. Given India's high solar irradiance and abundant reflective surfaces like desert sand, bifacial technology offers significant advantages for the country's solar expansion plans.
learn.stat4: Global bifacial market to reach $24B by 2030

learn.title: HVDC Transmission Lines Explained
learn.intro: High Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) transmission lines enable efficient long-distance power transfer across thousands of kilometers with minimal losses. Unlike traditional AC lines, HVDC can connect renewable-rich regions to demand centers, making it crucial for integrating large-scale renewable energy into national grids.
learn.c1_text: Think of HVDC as a high-speed pipeline for electricity. While AC power loses about 3% per 100 km due to inductive losses, HVDC loses only 1.5% per 100 km. This makes it ideal for transmitting solar power from Rajasthan to Delhi or wind energy from Tamil Nadu to northern India—distances where AC would be inefficient.
learn.c2_text: HVDC systems convert AC to DC at the sending end using rectifiers, transmit via two conductors, then convert back to AC at the receiving end with inverters. Modern Voltage Source Converter (VSC) technology allows precise power flow control and black-start capabilities, enabling grid stabilization and renewable energy integration.
learn.c3_text: India operates three major HVDC links: ±800 kV Raigarh-Pugal (1,500 km), ±500 kV Chandrapur-Kanyakumari (1,465 km), and ±600 kV Biyeskapatnam-Madhya Pradesh. These connect renewable-rich regions to industrial centers. The Green Energy Corridor project includes multiple HVDC lines to evacuate 50 GW renewable capacity by 2022.
learn.stat1: India has 5,000+ km HVDC transmission network
learn.stat2: HVDC losses: 1.5% per 100 km vs AC 3%

learn.title: Hydrogen Colours: Blue, Green, Grey
learn.intro: Hydrogen production methods determine its environmental impact, classified by color codes. Grey hydrogen comes from fossil fuels without carbon capture, blue includes carbon capture, and green uses renewable-powered electrolysis. Understanding these distinctions is vital for evaluating hydrogen's role in decarbonizing hard-to-abate sectors.
learn.c1_text: Grey hydrogen is like burning coal—it produces CO₂ as waste. Blue hydrogen adds carbon capture and storage (CCS), trapping 80-90% of emissions. Green hydrogen uses renewable electricity to split water, creating zero-emission fuel. Think of grey as smoking, blue as smoking with a filter, and green as vaping clean air.
learn.c2_text: Grey/blue hydrogen uses steam methane reforming (SMR): CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂, producing 9-12 kg CO₂ per kg H₂. Green hydrogen uses electrolysis: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂, requiring 50-55 kWh/kg H₂. Green costs $3-6/kg currently but will drop to $1-2/kg as renewables scale and electrolyzer costs decline.
learn.c3_text: India's National Green Hydrogen Mission allocates $2.3 billion to produce 5 MMT green hydrogen annually by 2030. Reliance Industries plans $70 billion investment in green hydrogen. IIT Bombay developed India's first hydrogen fuel cell bus. The mission targets reducing green H₂ cost to $1.5-2/kg, making it competitive with grey hydrogen.
learn.stat2: India targets 5 MMT green H₂/year by 2030
learn.stat3: Electrolysis needs 50-55 kWh per kg H₂

learn.title: Vehicle-to-Grid Technology Explained
learn.intro: Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) technology enables electric vehicles to act as mobile power plants, feeding electricity back to the grid during peak demand. With millions of EVs expected on roads globally, V2G could unlock massive distributed energy storage capacity, enhancing grid flexibility and accelerating renewable energy adoption.
learn.c1_text: Imagine your car's battery powering your home during a blackout or selling excess energy back to the grid. V2G-enabled EVs can discharge up to 10-20 kW of bidirectional power. A typical EV battery (60 kWh) could power an average home for 2-3 days or supply peak power to hundreds of homes collectively.
learn.c2_text: V2G requires specialized inverters and communication protocols between vehicles and grid operators. Using CHAdeMO or CCS standards with bidirectional capabilities, EVs can respond to grid signals within seconds. Aggregate fleets can provide frequency regulation, voltage support, and peak shaving services worth $500-1,500 annually per vehicle.
learn.c3_text: India's FAME scheme promotes EV adoption, with V2G pilot projects launched in Delhi and Mumbai. Tata Motors and Mahindra are developing V2G-compatible vehicles. IIT Madras created India's first V2G charger. With 2 million EVs projected by 2030, India could harness 120 GWh of distributed storage capacity through V2G technology.
learn.stat4: 2 million EVs could offer 120 GWh V2G capacity
